notes.definition: In a reaction between two reactants, the limiting reactant is the one that is completely used up. It limits the amount of product that can form. The other reactant is in excess, so some of it is left over at the end.
explanation: In a chemical reaction involving two reactants, it is common to use an excess of one of them. This makes sure that all of the other reactant is used up, which is useful if that reactant is expensive or if you want to be certain it all reacts. The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant, because it limits the amount of products that can be made. When it runs out, the reaction stops, even though some of the other reactant remains.

The amount of product formed is directly proportional to the amount of the limiting reactant. If you double the amount of limiting reactant (keeping the other reactant in excess), you double the amount of product. Adding more of the reactant that is already in excess does not make any more product, because there is nothing for the extra to react with.

To find which reactant is limiting, convert the mass of each reactant into moles (moles = mass ÷ Mr). Then use the balanced equation to compare the amounts with the ratio needed. For Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, 0.10 mol of magnesium needs 0.20 mol of HCl. If only 0.10 mol of HCl is present, the HCl runs out first, so HCl is the limiting reactant and magnesium is in excess.

A reliable method is: for one reactant, calculate how many moles of the other reactant it would need. If less than this is available, the other reactant is limiting. If more is available, the other reactant is in excess. Then always calculate the mass of product from the limiting reactant, using the mole ratio from the equation. Using the reactant in excess would give an answer that is too big.

You can also calculate how much of the excess reactant is left over: find the moles that react (from the limiting reactant and the ratio) and subtract from the moles you started with. Then convert to a mass if needed. In everyday terms, the limiting reactant is like the bread in a sandwich shop: if you have 10 slices of bread and 20 slices of cheese, you can only make 5 cheese sandwiches, and 15 slices of cheese are left.
keyFacts: The limiting reactant is completely used up in a reaction.
The limiting reactant determines (limits) the maximum amount of product.
The other reactant is in excess: some is left over at the end.
An excess of one reactant is often used to make sure all of the other reactant reacts.
Amount of product is directly proportional to the amount of limiting reactant.
Adding more of the excess reactant does not increase the amount of product.
To find the limiting reactant, convert masses to moles and compare with the mole ratio in the equation.
Always calculate the mass of product using the limiting reactant.

keyTerms.definition: The reactant that is completely used up in a reaction and so limits the amount of product formed.
More of a reactant than is needed to react with all of the other reactant; some is left over.
The ratio of moles of substances given by the coefficients in a balanced equation.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles too.
The largest amount of product that can form, calculated from the limiting reactant.
The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles.

equations.name: Number of moles
equations.formula: number of moles = mass in grams ÷ relative formula mass
equations.units: n in mol, m in g

workedExamples.title: Identifying the limiting reactant
workedExamples.question: 0.30 mol of magnesium is added to 0.40 mol of hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Which reactant is limiting, and how many moles of hydrogen are formed?
steps: 0.30 mol of Mg would need 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 mol of HCl.
Only 0.40 mol of HCl is present, so HCl runs out first: HCl is limiting.
Use HCl: ratio HCl : H₂ = 2 : 1, so moles of H₂ = 0.40 ÷ 2 = 0.20 mol.
Magnesium used = 0.20 mol, so 0.30 − 0.20 = 0.10 mol of magnesium is left over.
workedExamples.answer: HCl is limiting; 0.20 mol of hydrogen forms (0.10 mol of Mg is left).

workedExamples.title: Starting from masses
workedExamples.question: 5.6 g of iron is heated with 4.0 g of sulfur. Fe + S → FeS. Find the limiting reactant and the mass of iron sulfide formed. (Ar: S = 32, Fe = 56)
steps: Moles Fe = 5.6 ÷ 56 = 0.10 mol. Moles S = 4.0 ÷ 32 = 0.125 mol.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.10 mol Fe needs 0.10 mol S. There is 0.125 mol S, so sulfur is in excess and iron is limiting.
Moles FeS = 0.10 mol (from iron). Mr FeS = 88.
workedExamples.answer: Iron is limiting; 8.8 g of FeS forms and 0.80 g of sulfur is left over.

workedExamples.title: Unequal ratio
workedExamples.question: 4.0 g of hydrogen is mixed with 16 g of oxygen and ignited. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Calculate the mass of water formed. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Moles H₂ = 4.0 ÷ 2 = 2.0 mol. Moles O₂ = 16 ÷ 32 = 0.50 mol.
2.0 mol H₂ would need 1.0 mol O₂. Only 0.50 mol O₂ is present, so oxygen is limiting.
Ratio O₂ : H₂O = 1 : 2, so moles of water = 1.0 mol.
workedExamples.answer: 18 g of water (oxygen is limiting, 1.0 mol of H₂ is left over).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the reactant with the smaller mass is always the limiting reactant.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must compare moles using the ratio in the equation. 16 g of oxygen is limiting against only 4 g of hydrogen in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the reactant with fewer moles is always limiting.
misconceptions.right: In fact the mole ratio matters. With 0.10 mol Mg and 0.15 mol HCl in Mg + 2HCl, HCl is limiting even though there are more moles of it, because 0.10 mol Mg needs 0.20 mol HCl.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think adding more of any reactant will always make more product.
misconceptions.right: In fact only adding more of the limiting reactant increases the product. Extra excess reactant just stays unreacted.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often calculate the mass of product from whichever reactant is mentioned first.
misconceptions.right: In fact the mass of product must be calculated from the limiting reactant.

realWorld: In making medicines, the expensive starting material is usually the limiting reactant, with cheap reagents in excess so none of the valuable material is wasted.
Car engines are tuned so that petrol is the limiting reactant with oxygen from air in excess, so the fuel burns completely and less carbon monoxide is made.
In the Haber process, the ratio of nitrogen to hydrogen is controlled so that neither gas is wasted unnecessarily.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only: explaining the effect of a limiting quantity of a reactant on the amount of products in terms of moles or masses in grams.
examTips: Always convert masses to moles before deciding which reactant is limiting.
Use the balanced equation ratio: work out how many moles of the second reactant the first would need, then compare.
Calculate the product from the limiting reactant, never the one in excess.
In 'explain' questions, use the phrases 'completely used up', 'limits the amount of product' and 'in excess'.
If asked about doubling a reactant, say whether it is the limiting reactant: only then does the product double.
summary: The limiting reactant is completely used up and limits the product.
The other reactant is in excess and some is left over.
An excess is used to make sure all of the other reactant reacts.
Product amount is proportional to the limiting reactant.
Find the limiting reactant by comparing moles with the equation ratio.
Calculate product mass from the limiting reactant.

flashcards.back: The reactant that is completely used up and limits the amount of product.
There is more than enough of that reactant, so some is left over.

flashcards.front: Why do chemists often use one reactant in excess?
flashcards.back: To make sure all of the other (often more expensive) reactant reacts.

flashcards.front: What happens to the product if the limiting reactant is doubled?
flashcards.back: The amount of product doubles (if the other reactant is still in excess).

flashcards.front: What happens to the product if more of the excess reactant is added?
First step in finding the limiting reactant from masses?
flashcards.back: Convert each mass to moles (mass ÷ Mr).

flashcards.front: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: 0.1 mol Mg and 0.1 mol HCl. Which is limiting?
flashcards.back: HCl (0.1 mol Mg would need 0.2 mol HCl).

flashcards.front: Which reactant do you use to calculate the mass of product?
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 2 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂. Which is in excess?
flashcards.back: O₂ (2 mol H₂ needs only 1 mol O₂).

flashcards.front: How do you find the amount of excess reactant left over?
flashcards.back: Moles at start − moles that reacted (found from the limiting reactant and the ratio).

flashcards.front: Is the reactant with the smallest mass always limiting?
flashcards.back: No. Compare moles using the equation ratio.

questions.question: What is meant by the limiting reactant in a reaction?
options: The reactant with the smallest mass
The reactant that is completely used up
The reactant that is left over
The reactant with the largest Mr
markScheme: 1 mark: the reactant that is completely used up
questions.explanation: The limiting reactant runs out first and so limits the amount of product. The smallest mass is not always the limiting reactant.

questions.question: Why do chemists often use an excess of one reactant in a reaction?
options: To make more of the excess reactant
To make sure all of the other reactant is used up
To lower the mass of product
markScheme: 1 mark: to make sure all of the other reactant is used up
questions.explanation: An excess of one reactant ensures the other one reacts completely.

questions.question:
A student adds magnesium ribbon to excess hydrochloric acid.
Which reactant is the limiting reactant?
questions.explanation: If the acid is in excess, there is more than enough acid, so the magnesium is used up first and is limiting.

questions.question:
A student reacts zinc with excess sulfuric acid.
The student then doubles the mass of zinc. The acid is still in excess.
What happens to the volume of hydrogen produced?
questions.explanation: Zinc is limiting, and the amount of product is proportional to the amount of limiting reactant, so doubling the zinc doubles the hydrogen.

Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen:

A student mixes 2 mol of nitrogen with 3 mol of hydrogen.
Figure 1 represents the mixture.

questions.explanation: 2 mol of N₂ would need 6 mol of H₂. Only 3 mol is present, so hydrogen runs out first and 1 mol of N₂ is left.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
Table 1 shows four mixtures of magnesium and hydrochloric acid.
In which mixture is magnesium the limiting reactant?
questions.explanation: 0.10 mol of Mg needs 0.20 mol of HCl. Only in the last mixture is there more HCl than that, so Mg runs out first. In the others HCl is limiting.

questions.question:
Hydrogen reacts with oxygen:
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
A student mixes 4.0 g of hydrogen with 16 g of oxygen.
Which is the limiting reactant?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; O = 16
options: Neither, they are in the exact ratio
questions.explanation: H₂ = 2.0 mol, O₂ = 0.50 mol. 2.0 mol H₂ needs 1.0 mol O₂, but only 0.50 mol is present. Oxygen is limiting even though it has the larger mass.

questions.question:
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid:
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
10 g of CaCO₃ reacts with 0.10 mol of HCl.
What mass of CO₂ is produced?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16; Ca = 40
questions.explanation: CaCO₃ = 0.10 mol, which needs 0.20 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting. HCl : CO₂ = 2 : 1, so 0.050 mol CO₂ = 2.2 g. 4.4 g is the answer using CaCO₃ as limiting.

questions.question:
A student adds copper oxide, a little at a time, to 50 cm³ of sulfuric acid.
After a certain point, adding more copper oxide does not increase the mass of copper sulfate produced.
Which is the best explanation?
options: The copper oxide has become the limiting reactant
The sulfuric acid has been completely used up, so it is now limiting
The copper sulfate has stopped dissolving
markScheme: 1 mark: the sulfuric acid has been completely used up, so it is now limiting
questions.explanation: Once the acid is all used up, any extra copper oxide is in excess, so no more product can form.

questions.question:
Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
A student mixes 2 mol of nitrogen with 3 mol of hydrogen.
Calculate the maximum amount of ammonia that can be produced.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is limiting (2 mol N₂ would need 6 mol H₂). H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2, so 3 mol H₂ gives 2 mol NH₃.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
A student adds 0.30 mol of magnesium to 0.40 mol of HCl.
Calculate the amount of magnesium left over.
markScheme: 1 mark: HCl limiting; Mg reacting = 0.40 ÷ 2 = 0.20 mol
questions.explanation: 0.40 mol of HCl reacts with 0.20 mol of Mg, leaving 0.10 mol of Mg in excess.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
A student adds 0.10 mol of magnesium to 0.10 mol of HCl.
Calculate the amount of hydrogen produced.
markScheme: 1 mark: HCl is limiting (0.10 mol Mg needs 0.20 mol HCl)
questions.explanation: Using magnesium would give 0.10 mol, which is too big. HCl : H₂ = 2 : 1, so 0.050 mol.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with sulfur when heated:
Fe + S → FeS
A student heats a mixture of iron and sulfur.
Table 1 shows the masses of the reactants.
Calculate the mass of iron sulfide produced.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): S = 32; Fe = 56
questions.explanation: Ratio 1 : 1. Iron has fewer moles, so it is limiting. 0.10 mol FeS × 88 = 8.8 g.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with sulfur when heated:
Fe + S → FeS
A student heats a mixture of iron and sulfur. All the iron reacts.
Table 1 shows the masses of the reactants.
Calculate the mass of sulfur left over.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): S = 32; Fe = 56
questions.explanation: Only 0.10 mol of sulfur reacts with the 0.10 mol of iron; the rest, 0.80 g, is in excess.

questions.question:
Hydrogen reacts with oxygen:
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Table 1 shows the masses of the reactants in one reaction.
Calculate the maximum mass of water that can be produced.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; O = 16
questions.explanation: Hydrogen would need 1.0 mol of O₂ but only 0.50 mol is present. Using hydrogen would wrongly give 36 g.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with chlorine:
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
Table 1 shows the masses of the reactants in one reaction.
Calculate the mass of sodium chloride produced.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Na = 23; Cl = 35.5
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.10 mol Na needs only 0.050 mol Cl₂, so sodium is limiting
questions.explanation: Equal moles do not mean neither is limiting: the ratio is 2 : 1, so chlorine is in excess and sodium is limiting.

questions.question:
Magnesium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution:
Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu
A student adds 2.4 g of magnesium to a solution containing 0.050 mol of copper sulfate.
Calculate the mass of copper produced.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Mg = 24; Cu = 63.5
markScheme: 1 mark: copper sulfate is limiting (0.050 mol)
questions.explanation: The ratio is 1 : 1 and there is less copper sulfate, so 0.050 mol of Cu forms: 3.175 g = 3.18 g.

questions.question: What is meant by a reactant being 'in excess'?
markScheme: 1 mark: there is more of it than needed to react with all of the other reactant
1 mark: so some of it is left over at the end of the reaction
questions.explanation: The reactant in excess is not used up. The other reactant is the limiting reactant.

questions.question:
A student adds a piece of marble to excess acid.
Give one observation that shows the reaction has finished.
markScheme: 1 mark: the marble has disappeared (all used up) / fizzing stops
questions.explanation: The marble is limiting, so the reaction stops when it has all been used up and no more gas is made.

questions.question: Explain why adding more acid to a reaction does not increase the amount of product if the acid is already in excess.
markScheme: 1 mark: the other reactant is the limiting reactant / is already completely used up
1 mark: so the extra acid has nothing to react with; the amount of product depends on the limiting reactant
questions.explanation: The limiting reactant controls the maximum amount of product.

questions.question: Suggest why, in making a medicine, the expensive starting material is usually the limiting reactant.
acceptedAnswers: so none of it is wasted
markScheme: 1 mark: a cheaper reactant is used in excess
1 mark: so all of the expensive starting material reacts and none is wasted
questions.explanation: Leaving cheap reactant over costs little, but leaving expensive reactant unreacted wastes money.

questions.question:
Magnesium burns in oxygen:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
A student burns 0.50 mol of magnesium in 0.50 mol of oxygen.
Identify the limiting reactant.
Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.50 mol Mg needs only 0.25 mol O₂, so oxygen is in excess
questions.explanation: Although the moles are equal, the 2 : 1 ratio means magnesium is used up first.

questions.question:
Methane burns in oxygen:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
8.0 g of methane is burned in 24 g of oxygen.
Show which reactant is the limiting reactant.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; C = 12; O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.50 mol CH₄ needs 1.0 mol O₂
1 mark: only 0.75 mol available, so oxygen is limiting
questions.explanation: Oxygen runs out before all the methane has burned, so some methane is left (and in a real flame, incomplete combustion is likely).

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
A student says:
'The reactant with the smaller number of moles is always the limiting reactant.'
Explain why the student is wrong. Use this reaction as an example.
acceptedAnswers: HCl can be limiting even with more moles
markScheme: 1 mark: you must compare using the mole ratio in the equation
1 mark: for example 0.10 mol Mg with 0.15 mol HCl: Mg has fewer moles but needs 0.20 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting
questions.explanation: When the coefficients are not 1 : 1, the reactant with more moles can still run out first.

questions.question:
A student adds different masses of magnesium ribbon to 50 cm³ portions of the same hydrochloric acid.
The student measures the volume of hydrogen produced each time.
Figure 1 shows the results.
Explain the shape of the graph. Use ideas about the limiting reactant.

Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one part explained, or a simple statement such as 'the acid runs out'.
questions.explanation: The plateau shows the point where acid, not magnesium, limits the amount of hydrogen.

questions.question:
Aluminium reacts with chlorine:
2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃
Table 1 shows the masses of the reactants a chemist uses.
Determine the limiting reactant.
Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium chloride that can be produced and the mass of the excess reactant left over.
Explain your reasoning at each stage.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Al = 27; Cl = 35.5
markScheme: Indicative content: moles Al = 2.7 ÷ 27 = 0.10 mol; moles Cl₂ = 14.2 ÷ 71 = 0.20 mol; 0.10 mol Al needs 0.10 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.15 mol Cl₂; 0.20 mol available, so chlorine is in excess and aluminium is limiting; moles AlCl₃ = 0.10 mol (ratio 2 : 2); Mr AlCl₃ = 27 + 106.5 = 133.5; mass = 0.10 × 133.5 = 13.35 g (13.4 g); Cl₂ left = 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.050 mol = 0.050 × 71 = 3.55 g; check: 2.7 + 14.2 = 16.9 g = 13.35 + 3.55 g.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct limiting reactant with reasoning, correct mass of product and correct mass of excess chlorine, clearly explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): limiting reactant correctly identified and one further calculation correct.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): moles of one or both reactants correct with little further progress.
questions.explanation: Aluminium is limiting (it needs only 0.15 mol of the 0.20 mol of chlorine). 13.35 g of AlCl₃ forms and 3.55 g of chlorine is left, which together equal the 16.9 g of reactants.
